Ananda Geyser-Fouché and Ebele Chukwuka': Ananda Geyser-Fouché and Ebele Chukwuka's article in HTS Teologiese Studies calls 1 Chronicles 21 a much-debated text, primarily because of the presence of Satan or satan. Barnett's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia reads the verse as showing that the Chronicler knew a personal principle of evil that warred against God. Andrew Perrin lists Daniel 2:4b–7:28 amo: Andrew Perrin lists Daniel 2:4b–7:28 among the biblical texts composed in Aramaic. Annette Yoshiko Reed's Fallen Angels ref: Annette Yoshiko Reed's Fallen Angels refers to the quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9 in the Epistle of Jude, and Kelley Coblentz Bautch says a selection from the Book of the Watchers is quoted in Jude 14–15. Another significant example of the adult: Another significant example of the adulterous-woman motif appears in Num 5:11-31, where the law allows a man who suspects his wife of adultery to make her undergo an ordeal in front of the priest to test whether or not she has been unfaithful. As a result, during the recent decades t: As a result, during the recent decades the researchers have generally agreed that the exceptionally rich narrative of Abraham in Gen 11:27–25:11 does not constitute a legacy of any oral tradition from the period of the monarchy, but a fruit of theological and literary labours by the circles interested in the figure during the captivity period, and afterwards.

Sefer ha-Berit), name derived from Exodus 24:7 ("And he took the book of the covenant, and read it aloud to the people.…"), and usually taken to refer to the legal, moral, and cultic corpus of literature found in Exodus 20:22–23:33. Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article: Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article says some of the latest texts of the Hebrew Bible start using names for angels, such as Gabriel and Michael in Daniel, written in the second century BCE. Bernard Bamberger's entry in the Encyclopaedia Judaica says that in Daniel the angels now have proper names, that it is the only biblical book in which angels have distinct personalities, and that it is the first in which each nation has an angelic patron. Gershom Scholem's entry says Raphael first appears as an angel's name in Tobit 12:15 and 1 Enoch 20:3, where he is one of the seven archangels, and Joshua Gutmann's says later apocalyptic writings name Uriel and others as interpreters of visions. Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article says the Hebrew Bible provides ample evidence that many Israelites believed in the existence of multiple deities, and that even some authors of the biblical texts seem polytheistic; it refers to many heavenly creatures, calling them “gods” (Genesis 6:2; Psalms 29:1; 82:6; 86:8; 89:7; Job 1:6). S. David Sperling's Encyclopedia of Religion entry says some biblical writers took the existence of other gods for granted, though all agreed that Yahveh was superior to the other gods. Christine Hayes's Yale lectures call it simply a fact that practices and ideas that are not strictly or even strongly monotheistic appear in the Bible, and Peter Machinist writes that the Hebrew Bible, while it gives evidence of monotheism, especially in Second Isaiah, also tells of polytheism. Debra Scoggins Ballentine's Bible Odyssey article describes many divine beings in the Hebrew Bible who are subservient to Yahweh, among them the Host of Heaven, the “holy ones” and the “sons of God”.

Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article says the Hebrew mal'akh, like the Greek angelos, means “messenger”; the Hebrew Bible occasionally uses it of a human messenger, but typically of heavenly beings who serve Yhwh. Stephen White's article in the Tyndale Bulletin says the word means messenger or representative, both human and divine. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry by Bernard Bamberger says the term is frequently applied to human agents, that the Greek angelos has the same range of meanings, and that the word took on the exclusive meaning “angel” only when it passed through Latin into other European languages; it also says the angel is often called simply “man”. T. L. Fallon's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia says angels sent by God appeared for the most part in human form, and that only one angel in the Bible is said to be able to fly (Daniel 9:21).
Beyond these sources found in 1 Samuel,: Beyond these sources found in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel 9–20 and 1 Kings 1–2 primarily draw from another hypothetical source called the “Succession Narrative.” This source is so named because it presumably was composed as an explanation of how and why Solomon became David’s heir.

Breed writes that scholars think many of: Breed writes that scholars think many of the Old Greek translators worked from early Hebrew versions of biblical books that were quite different from those that became the Masoretic Text, and that discoveries in the Dead Sea region show these alternate Hebrew versions circulated alongside the versions that became the Masoretic Text. When the Greek translation was made, he adds, there was no Masoretic Text or any official Bible, only multiple editions of many scrolls. Samuel Thomas's Bible Odyssey answer agrees that in some cases the Hebrew text behind the Septuagint was clearly different from, and perhaps earlier than, the Masoretic Text, and points to certain manuscripts among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Davies's Encyclopaedia Judaica entry reports Qumran manuscripts of Isaiah that support Septuagint readings and Hebrew copies of the shorter edition of Jeremiah known from the Septuagint. Translators also made choices of their own. Discussing how the Greek renders the Hebrew word ‘almah, Thomas cautions that it is sometimes difficult to say why a particular scribe or translator made a particular decision, and notes that in Isaiah 7:14 the translator had several choices for translation.
Breed writes that until the last few dec: Breed writes that until the last few decades most biblical scholars believed the Masoretic texts were, with some exceptions, the best witnesses to the most ancient Hebrew text, and that the Dead Sea Scrolls have since suggested several different versions of many books. Thomas writes that recent gains in textual criticism mean we can no longer say whether the Septuagint or the Masoretic Text represents a more original text, if such a thing can even be spoken of, at least in the case he discusses, Psalm 16:10. Davies's entry says that in a few cases a Qumran reading is clearly superior to the Masoretic Text; his example is Deuteronomy 32:8, where a Qumran manuscript agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text.
Brettler says many scholars believe the: Brettler says many scholars believe the laws of Exodus 34:10–26, often named the Cultic Decalogue, were the original or earliest Decalogue. Sherman says many contemporary scholars now reject Julius Wellhausen's claim that Exodus 34 contains an ancient Ritual Decalogue, and argue that the whole chapter is a late compilation that draws on earlier laws; she says its festival and ritual laws are very close to those of the Covenant Code and end with exactly the same laws, while adding expansions that connect them to other legal collections. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's article on the Decalogue, in text carried over from its first edition, reports that critics regarded the Exodus 34 list as the more ancient, and questions the basis of that dating.
Brown says Deuteronomy's Sabbath command: Brown says Deuteronomy's Sabbath commandment makes no mention of God's work of creation and instead grounds the Sabbath in Israel's slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). But on closer examination, the definitio: But on closer examination, the definition of adultery in much of the Hebrew Bible is one-sided. Men did not have to be faithful to one woman. But such marriages could nevertheless le: But such marriages could nevertheless lead to love: Jacob loved Rachel (Gen 29:20, Gen 29:30) and Michal loved David (1Sam 18:20).

By this view, the reason for “seven clea: By this view, the reason for “seven clean” animals in one tradition is that Noah will offer a sacrifice following the flood (Gen 8:20), whereas in the other tradition, which is often associated with priestly interests in ancient Israel, no such sacrifice will be offered since sacrifice is the exclusive domain of priests.
Carol Meyers's Bible Odyssey article say: Carol Meyers's Bible Odyssey article says close study revealed biblical narratives to be replete with inconsistencies and even outright contradictions: in 1 Samuel 17:50 David kills Goliath, but in 2 Samuel 21:19 Elhanan does, and Joshua says the Israelites conquered the whole land while Judges describes the survival of many Canaanites; Hayes's lecture on Joshua and Judges adds that Judges 1 gives a long list of the places from which the Canaanites were not expelled. Carol Meyers's Encyclopaedia Judaica art: Carol Meyers's Encyclopaedia Judaica article describes levirate marriage as one in which a childless widow married her deceased husband's brother, the first son of that union being counted the dead man's heir (Deuteronomy 25:5–10; compare Tamar in Genesis 38, and Ruth). Christine Hayes says Belshazzar was neve: Christine Hayes says Belshazzar was never king but a prince regent, defeated by Cyrus, not Darius, that the Median king Darius is unknown to history, and that these inaccuracies are a sign of a much later writer looking back. Christine Hayes's Yale lecture says Hose: Christine Hayes's Yale lecture says Hosea condemns Israel's religious faithlessness in terms of adultery, through the metaphor of a marriage in which Israel is the unfaithful, adulterous wife. Stuart Macwilliam's Bible Odyssey article says some scholars attempt to rehabilitate the texts, but that feminist scholars have led the way in exposing the damage the metaphor causes; Tamar Kamionkowski's Jewish Women's Archive article says some recent commentators have called Ezekiel 16 and 23 “pornoprophetic”. Christine Hayes's Yale lecture says ther: Christine Hayes's Yale lecture says there are in fact two creation stories in Genesis, with quite a few contradictions between them: the first, in Genesis 1, concludes in Genesis 2:4, and the second begins in Genesis 2:4 and runs into Genesis 3. Shalom Paul's Encyclopaedia Judaica entry calls them the P and J accounts according to the documentary hypothesis and says their sources reflect different epic traditions. The textbook summary for the next chapter adds that, although the evidence does not fit the classical form of the hypothesis as neatly as scholars once thought, almost all biblical scholars recognize that the Pentateuch's repetitions, inconsistencies and contradictions are best explained by distinct sources from different periods.
Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say Dani: Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say Daniel 12 imagines a resurrection of the dead as compensation to those who died under the persecutions of Antiochus, and is the only passage of the Bible to explicitly espouse an individual life after death. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the idea of individual resurrection first appears in Daniel 12:2–3, written about 167 BCE. The New American Bible's notes say biblical books begin to speak positively of life with God after death in the second century BCE, and that Daniel distinguishes two groups, one rising to eternal life, the other to reproach and disgrace. Stephen Cook's Bible Odyssey article says Daniel 12:2 is not the earliest Jewish text about the dead rising, since 1 Enoch 27:1–4 reflects earlier ideas, and that texts such as Isaiah 26:19 show that some in Israel likely already believed in bodily resurrection by the exile. The UBS handbook on Isaiah says commentators generally agree that Isaiah 26:19 speaks of the resurrection of the dead, but that its language may be a figure for the restoration of the nation, which is how the New American Bible's note reads it.
Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say that: Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say that although many later Hellenistic Jewish texts and the New Testament identify the snake as a Satan, in Genesis 3 it is simply a talking animal. Brad Anderson's Bible Odyssey article says the text does not reveal the serpent's nature or identity, that the serpent's association with evil became common in Judaism in the Second Temple period (1 Enoch, the Life of Adam and Eve), and that it was not a long stretch for readers to equate it with Satan. The New American Bible calls Wisdom 2:24 the first biblical text to equate the serpent of Genesis 3 with the devil, and says Christian tradition identified the snake with the devil, citing also John 8:44 and Revelation 12:9 and 20:2. Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey talk says biblical scholars think the “ancient serpent” of Revelation is the serpent of the ancient Near Eastern combat myth, and that the associations of Satan are not brought together with the serpent in the garden until early Christian writings.
Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say the: Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say the outcry God hears is against the Sodomites' violation of the law of hospitality to strangers and their desire to gang rape them, and that the idea that Sodom's fundamental sin was homosexual behavior is not present in the Hebrew Bible but appears only in later documents. J. Stiebert's article in Verbum et Ecclesia says what is at issue is primarily gang rape and the humiliation of male visitors, in Genesis 19 and the similar story in Judges 19, and reads Ezekiel 16:49 as condemning Sodom for pride, social injustice and lack of hospitality. Jan Joosten's article in the Journal of Theological Studies says the projected sex is condemned because it was not consensual. Rhiannon Graybill's Bible Odyssey article on Judges 19 says the focus is on the failure to show hospitality, with rape threats used to establish dominance over male foreigners. Eoghan Ahern's article in the Journal of the History of Sexuality says studies have shown the homosexual reading of Sodom was an addition of later commentators. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary records both attempted sexual perversity and gross inhospitality in the story. Cephas Tushima's article in Old Testament Essays notes that others continue to hold the traditional view, and reads Lot's offer of his daughters as a response to the idea of men having sex with men.
Christo Lombaard's article in Scriptura: Christo Lombaard's article in Scriptura says Hosea 12 has been widely accepted as the first reference to the patriarchs outside the Pentateuch, usually dated to the time of the prophet Hosea in the mid-8th century BCE; Lombaard himself argues that the passage is later than 538 BCE. Janusz Lemański says scholars tend to agree that the text of Hosea attests the authenticity of the tradition associated with Jacob, and assigns chronological priority to the Jacob tradition. Israel Finkelstein's The Forgotten Kingdom calls the core of the Jacob cycle probably the earliest material in the patriarchal stories, representing a time before the collapse of the northern kingdom. On Abraham, Lemański says researchers in recent decades have generally agreed that the Abraham narrative of Genesis 11:27–25:11 is not a legacy of oral tradition from the monarchy but the work of circles active during the captivity and after, and Lombaard writes that scholars already accept Abraham as a primarily exilic or post-exilic figure. Finkelstein, in The Quest for the Historical Israel, speaks instead of pre-exilic sources of the patriarchal narratives, a literary attempt to redefine the unity of Israel in the late Iron Age II. The New American Bible's introduction to Genesis says scholars have traditionally dated the stories to the first half of the second millennium BCE, though a few regard them as late, from the sixth or fifth century BCE, and purely fictional. Konrad Schmid argues in Biblica that the ancestor stories of Genesis and the Moses story were originally autonomous literary units, a view he says has gained increased acceptance, especially in European scholarship; Lemański says it remains unsolved when the patriarchal traditions were combined with the Exodus, though most scholars lean toward the Priestly school as the milieu that merged them.
Clement of Alexandria seems to be the fi: Clement of Alexandria seems to be the first to have linked 1 Peter 3:19 with the descent of Christ
Close study of biblical narratives revea: Close study of biblical narratives revealed that they are replete with inconsistencies and even outright contradictions. For example, humans are created before vegetation in Gen 2:4-9 but afterward in Gen 1:11-27. Or in 1Sam 17:50, David kills Goliath, whereas in 2Sam 21:19, Elhanan does.
Commentators generally agree that it spe: Commentators generally agree that it speaks about the resurrection of the dead. If so, it is a unique statement in the Old Testament. However, the language here may be figurative. The dead may be those who have gone or will go into exile, so that resurrection is actually a figure for the restoration of the nation of Judah, as in Ezek 37.
Concern for heirs is also a factor in th: Concern for heirs is also a factor in the institution known as levirate marriage, in which a childless widow would marry her deceased husband's brother, with the first son produced by that liaison considered the dead man's heir (Deut. 25:5–10; cf. the narratives of Tamar, Gen. 38, and Ruth).
Contrary to the prevailing scholarly vie: Contrary to the prevailing scholarly view that the pericope’s intrinsic function is to provide the rationale for the flood narrative, I contend that Genesis 6:1–4 was originally an independent tradition with no direct connection to the flood story.
Coogan and Chapman's textbook summary sa: Coogan and Chapman's textbook summary says Second Isaiah emphasises strict monotheism, and that it is the first passage in the Bible to state explicitly that there is no God other than Yahweh; the summary dates Second Isaiah to the sixth century, in Babylon. The New American Bible's note on Isaiah 44:6 says that with Second Isaiah, Israel's faith is declared to be explicitly monotheistic, while earlier formulas, not even the first commandment, did not exclude the existence of other gods. Hayes's lectures say the monotheism implicit in Isaiah becomes quite explicit in Second Isaiah, and Sperling calls Second Isaiah the most consistent monotheist among the prophets, insisting that Yahveh was the sole god in existence. Sperling writes that scholars are in agreement that Judaism was a monotheistic religion by the end of the Babylonian exile, about 539 BCE, and that the present state of the evidence suggests that monolatry arose early in Israel but monotheism was a late development. Dominik Markl finds the earliest evidence of the explicit claim in Deuteronomy 4 and Second Isaiah, both likely composed around or some time after 539 BCE, and notes that whether Deuteronomy 4 comes first is a matter of debate. Peter Machinist reports that, depending on the scholar, monotheism in the strict sense could be as late as the exile, and that for those who date it late, Second Isaiah has been the favoured option. Other scholars date it differently. Baruch Levine places the transition to what he calls global monotheism, the concept that Yahweh is the only God and rules over all nations, in the late eighth to early seventh century BCE. Markl reports that Sven Petry concluded monotheism was introduced in Second Isaiah no earlier than the fifth century BCE. Paula Fredriksen writes that in biblical narrative other divine forces are often simply there, and reads declarations of God's unique supremacy, such as Deuteronomy 4:35, 39 and Isaiah 43:10–11; 44:6; 45:14, as an index of a people's cultic and affective loyalty, like similar statements about pagan gods.

Coogan and Chapman's textbook summary says the first commandment stipulates that only Yahweh is to be worshipped by Israel, which presupposes not monotheism but monolatry, the worship of one god while not denying the existence of others. The New American Bible's note on Exodus 20:3 says the commandment is traditionally understood as an outright denial that any god but the God of Israel exists, but that in the context of the prohibitions in verses 4–5 it is more precisely God's demand for Israel's exclusive worship and allegiance. William P. Brown's Bible Odyssey article says the Decalogue assumes the existence of other gods. Ronald Hendel's Encyclopedia of Religion entry says early biblical texts seem to acknowledge that the gods of other nations exist, and that this seems to be the earliest sense of the first commandment. Baruch Levine, who calls this belief henotheism, writes that it is proclaimed in the Decalogue's “You shall have no other gods in my presence”, which in his numbering is the second commandment.
Critics have called the stipulations of: Critics have called the stipulations of Exodus 34 the "cultic decalogue," as distinguished from the traditional – or the "ethical" – decalogue, and regard it as the more ancient. This relative dating rests in large measure on the supposition that the "ethical decalogue" reflects the teachings of the literary prophets.
Dale Martin's Yale lecture uses the divo: Dale Martin's Yale lecture uses the divorce sayings to illustrate how scholars test sayings of the historical Jesus: Mark, a saying from Q in Matthew 5:32 and Luke 16:18, and Paul give three separate, independent witnesses that Jesus taught against divorce, and the saying is dissimilar to the practice of the very writers who pass it on and then modify it. John Martens writes that there is no real doubt that Jesus prohibited divorce, and that Mary Rose D'Angelo's argument that the sayings do not go back to Jesus has found few if any followers; in Mark, he writes, remarriage after divorce, common in ancient Judaism and the wider Mediterranean world, counts as adultery. A. Andrew Das's Bible Odyssey article says that Jesus appeals to the creation story to prohibit divorce, and that unlike the general social practice of the time the New Testament authors forbade divorce with few exceptions.
Dale Martin's Yale lectures say some rea: Dale Martin's Yale lectures say some readers take Romans 1 as a condemnation of modern homosexuality and believe that is a sound historical reading, while others, using the same historical-critical methods, say homosexuality is not Paul's concern. William Loader's HTS article reports that Robert Gagnon, as do many in current debates, distinguishes homosexual orientation from the act and argues that Paul's focus is the act. Bruce Wells calls Gagnon's 2001 book the older, more conservative view and says the more progressive views of Jennifer Knust's and Michael Coogan's books are accepted by most academic scholars today.
Dale Martin's Yale lectures say some sch: Dale Martin's Yale lectures say some scholars hold that the verses in 1 Corinthians 14 teaching the subordination of women were a later scribal interpolation, while other scholars disagree and think they were original. Richard Fellows's article in New Testament Studies says the verses appear after 14:40 in the Western tradition, a fact that, with other evidence, has led many to see them as a non-Pauline addition, perhaps first a note in the margin. The NABRE notes say all manuscripts contain the verses, though some move them to the end of the chapter. Philip Payne argues that marks in Codex Vaticanus identify the verses as added text, and that a marginal gloss best explains their two locations; Fellows replies that the mark Payne reads is indistinguishable from an ordinary paragraph mark, and says he does not address whether Paul wrote the verses.
Dan 12:1-3 provides the first reference: Dan 12:1-3 provides the first reference to the idea of individual resurrection found in the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament.
Daniel 12:2, a text written in the secon: Daniel 12:2, a text written in the second century B.C.E., is not the earliest Jewish text about the dead rising. 1 Enoch 27:1-4 reflects even earlier Jewish ideas about resurrection. Texts such as Isa 26:19, Isa 53:11 (see NIV), and Ps 22:29 (see NAB) all show that some in Israel likely already believed in bodily resurrection by the Babylonian exile.
David Frankel writes that most scholars: David Frankel writes that most scholars by now agree that the elohim who come under divine judgment and are condemned to death in Psalm 82 are not human leaders or judges but divine beings, members of a divine council, and that the traditional interpretation of them as human judges was defended by Yehezkel Kaufmann. Erica Mongé-Greer writes that discussion of the psalm has focused on the identity of the figures named in its first verse, and that there has been no clear consensus. Janusz Lemański describes three proposed interpretations, among them a literal reading of the elohim as pagan gods dethroned in favour of the one true God, and one that takes them as human authorities such as judges or rulers; he advocates the literal reading himself. Roland Owusu-Ansah and his co-authors find good reason to identify the elohim as gods, though the psalm's history of interpretation includes proposals such as human judges. The New American Bible's note reads the gods as subordinate divine beings to whom Israel's God had delegated oversight of foreign countries, now stripped of divine status and reduced to mortals; its note on verse 8 says God will now directly take over the rulership of the whole world. When the psalm was written is also disputed: Mongé-Greer says scholars widely disagree about when, where and why it exists, and Lemański, while saying the data are not sufficient to date it precisely, finds the end of the exile the most probable date.
Devil: the first biblical text to equate: Devil: the first biblical text to equate the serpent of Gn 3 with the devil.
Divorce could take place for a variety o: Divorce could take place for a variety of reasons and did not necessarily require specific grounds. Deuteronomy 24:3, for example, describes a man divorcing his wife simply because he “dislikes her.”
During the monarchical period, it became: During the monarchical period, it became the site of an infamous high place, where some of the kings of Judah engaged in forbidden religious practices, including human sacrifice by fire (2Chr 28:3; 2Chr 33:6; Jer 7:31; Jer 32:35).
Early LGBTQ+ interpretation focused prim: Early LGBTQ+ interpretation focused primarily on challenging heterosexist and cis-normative readings of a collection of biblical passages commonly called the “clobber passages” (e.g., Gen 19:1–11; Lev 18:22; 20:13; Rom 1:26–28; 1 Cor 6:9–10; 1 Tim 1:9–10).
Early biblical texts seem to acknowledge: Early biblical texts seem to acknowledge that gods of other nations exist (Dt. 32:8). The nations each have their own god, but Yahweh is Israel's god. This seems to be the earliest sense of the first commandment, "You shall have no other gods beside me" (Ex. 20:3).
Eastern Christians resisted this conflat: Eastern Christians resisted this conflation, traditionally regarding the two Marys as distinct saints. In the West, however, Pope Gregory the Great pronounced, in the sixth century, that the “sinner” Mary who anointed Jesus’ feet (Luke 7:36-50) was Mary Magdalene rather than Mary of Bethany.
Elizabeth Schrader's article in the Harv: Elizabeth Schrader's article in the Harvard Theological Review sets out to show that the first circulating version of John may not have included Martha, and that Papyrus 66 may give a window onto a late scribal interpolation. She says the correction of 11:3 in Papyrus 66 clearly splits one woman into two, and that 17 of the 92 Greek witnesses she surveyed for John 11:1–12:2 contain traces of Martha's absence; she suggests there is a strong possibility that Martha was added to hamper the text's subtle identification of Mary of Bethany with Mary Magdalene. Richard Fellows, in TC: A Journal of Biblical Textual Criticism, repeats Schrader's point that Martha was absent from 11:1–3 in Papyrus 66 before it was corrected, notes that it is no longer clear whether the name erased at 11:3 was Mary or Martha, and argues that the variants are better explained by a sexist tendency and harmonising than by interpolation: someone wanting to denigrate Mary would not have placed her before Martha at 11:1 and before Lazarus at 11:5, and Schrader's proposed first text combines too many weakly attested and unattested readings. In a 2025 exchange in the same journal, Schrader Polczer holds that Martha's interpolation remains a compelling explanation, and Fellows replies that there is no text-critical case for it. Fellows notes that Papyrus 66 is dated to about 200 CE by the Nestle-Aland edition, though Brent Nongbri argues it could be as late as the fourth century.
Ellen White's Bible Odyssey article defi: Ellen White's Bible Odyssey article defines a divine council, at its simplest, as a gathering of gods: a governing body convened to make decisions, with a clearly established hierarchy under the most powerful god in attendance. She points to the texts from Ugarit, whose pantheon has four clear tiers with El and Asherah at the top, and to similar councils in Egypt, Mesopotamia, Canaan, Phoenicia and Greece. In the Hebrew Bible, White says, God Most High has a divine council in Deuteronomy 32:8 (see also Psalm 82:1), and six passages present the workings of Yahweh's council: 1 Kings 22:19–23; Job 1:6–12; 2:1–7; Isaiah 6; Zechariah 3; Daniel 7. Obioma Agharanya and Felix Poniatowski list 1 Kings 22:19–23, Isaiah 6, Job 1–2, Psalm 82, Zechariah 3 and Daniel 7:9–14 as passages that raise little doubt as genuine depictions of the divine council, and say they are generally recognised in scholarship as belonging to that genre. The New American Bible's note on Genesis 1:26 says that in the ancient Near East, and sometimes in the Bible, God was imagined as presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings who deliberated about matters on earth, which it says accounts for the plural forms in that verse and in Genesis 11:7; its note on 1 Kings 22 says prophets stand in the council of the Lord and are privy to its deliberations. Hayes says Yahweh is represented in many passages as presiding over a council of gods, and White notes that the biblical divine council often mirrors the human royal court familiar to the biblical authors.
Elsewhere in the Deuteronomistic History: Elsewhere in the Deuteronomistic History, use of teraphim is condemned (15:23; 2 Kgs 23:24).
Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation epi: Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation epic, tells how the god Marduk defeats Tiamat, the primeval salt-water ocean, and builds the world from her carcass. Kacie Klamm's Bible Odyssey article says it was likely composed in the second millennium BCE, long before the earliest parts of the Bible were written down. Hayes points to the resemblances: Genesis 1 opens with a temporal clause, as the epic does, has a wind sweep over chaotic waters as Marduk's wind was released into the face of Tiamat, and has God set up the heavenly bodies, as Marduk did. Klamm adds that Genesis 1 runs over seven days and the epic over seven tablets, and that humans are made on the sixth day and in the sixth tablet. Paul's entry finds the same sequence of events in both, firmament, dry land, luminaries, humans and divine rest, and concludes that at least the P account appears to echo the earlier Babylonian story. The Coogan and Chapman summary likewise says Enuma Elish shares a number of affinities with Genesis 1. There are differences too. In Genesis, Hayes says, there is no battle: a listener who knew the old story would hear the wind and the watery deep, and then only a word, “let there be light”. Hayes and the Coogan and Chapman summary describe Genesis 1 as demythologizing the older material; Paul writes that Genesis totally rejects mythology and that the differences are much more striking than the similarities. In Enuma Elish, Hayes says, service was imposed on humans so that the gods were free; in Genesis 1 the creation of humans is the climactic act, and they are given rule over the other creatures. Klamm reports that scholars explain the similarities differently: some biblical writers may have known the epic, given Babylon's power, while others think both texts drew on common ancient Near Eastern beliefs.
Eve Levavi Feinstein's Bible Odyssey art: Eve Levavi Feinstein's Bible Odyssey article says that in all references to divorce in the Hebrew Bible it is initiated by the husband, as Deuteronomy 24:1–4 assumes, but that it is not known for certain that Israelite women could not initiate divorce: ancient Near Eastern law codes and contracts suggest it may have been possible in certain times and places, and Jewish women initiated divorce at Elephantine in Egypt in the fifth century BCE. She writes that divorce did not necessarily require specific grounds: Deuteronomy 24:3 describes a man divorcing his wife because he “dislikes her”. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says a marriage could be ended by the husband with a written bill of divorce, and that there was no law among biblical Israelites allowing the woman to initiate divorce. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's article on Elephantine says divorce there could be effected at the request of either husband or wife. The NABRE note on Deuteronomy 24:1–4 says the law directly forbids a divorced man from remarrying his former wife and indirectly checks hasty divorces, while taking divorce itself for granted. John Martens writes that Jewish thinkers did not usually question the propriety of divorce but debated acceptable reasons for it, and David Instone-Brewer that Hillel, in the first century BCE, allowed men to divorce their wives on the ground called “any matter”.
Even when Elohim refers to the God of Is: Even when Elohim refers to the God of Israel, it can be treated as a plural (Gn. 20:13).
Exodus 6:2-4, a very important passage,: Exodus 6:2-4, a very important passage, is assigned to P, and here God says, "I am [Yahweh]. I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as El Shaddai, but I did not make Myself known to them by My name [Yahweh]."
Extra-biblical records and accounts sugg: Extra-biblical records and accounts suggest that some materials from the first half of the book of Daniel may be based on Neo-Babylonian realities. Notably, Nebuchadnezzar’s exile (Dan 4) may have been based on the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus. There is even an extra-biblical account of Nabonidus consulting with a Jewish seer, as Nebuchadnezzar does in chapter 4. Yet the extra-biblical account does not name Daniel.
Finally, the replacement tablets given t: Finally, the replacement tablets given to Moses after breaking the first set contain a significantly different set of laws (Exod 34:1-28).
Finkelstein calls the great united monar: Finkelstein calls the great united monarchy a literary construct of late-monarchic Judahite authors, and Brian Schmidt's summary of his argument ties it to a later Josianic ideal of uniting the two states under Jerusalem. Sergi says political unity between Israel and Judah could only be imagined after Israel fell in 720 BCE. Nakhai says some scholars read the Bible's united kingdom as an elegy to a long-lost national unity, and the Encyclopaedia Judaica's history entry that the biblical writers sometimes projected the events and institutions of their own time onto earlier times. Nadav Na'aman says most scholars of Israel's early history have treated the account of David's conquests in 2 Samuel 8 as late historiography that does not reflect the ancient reality, and himself supports the view that David's conquests there were modelled on the victories of foreign kings. On what lies behind the picture, Finkelstein suggests the seed may have been Jerusalem's chiefs taking over the former Saulide territories, and Schmidt reports his view that if any Israelite kingdom ever united north and south, it was the Omride kingdom ruled from Samaria in the ninth century; Sergi roots the idea of unity under David in the actual unity of Judah and Benjamin under the house of David in the early Iron IIA. Mazar holds that parts of the account, such as the description of Jerusalem's temple and the mention of Sheshonq's campaign, could not have been invented in the seventh century or later.
Following Fitzmyer, and others, I believ: Following Fitzmyer, and others, I believe this exception clause was first concerned with marriages which ought not to have been contracted due to degrees of consanguinity outlawed by Leviticus 18
For Lev 18:18 is cryptic. Hence, the dis: For Lev 18:18 is cryptic. Hence, the dispute as to whether it means to ban polygyny (CD) or else to prohibit the marriage of a man to a woman and her biological sister (the builders of the partition who permit polygyny). To be sure, CD’s understanding of Lev 18:18 languished for umpteen centuries, but that has not prevented scholars, Angelo Tosato amongst them, from re-opening the case.
For example, God, the Most High (literal: For example, God, the Most High (literally El Elyon), is said to have a divine council in Deut 32:8 (see also Ps 82:1). There are also six passages in the Old Testament that present the workings of Yahweh’s Council (1Kgs 22:19–23; Job 1:6–12; 2:1–7; Isa 6; Zech 3; Dan 7).
For example, the story of Joseph (Gen 37: For example, the story of Joseph (Gen 37-50) is often called a “diaspora story” because although its final form was written within the land of Israel, it describes how Joseph learns to survive outside his homeland.
For the most part, the angels sent by Go: For the most part, the angels sent by God to intervene in men's lives appeared to them in human form (Gn 18.2; 19.1; Dn 8.15).
For these passages are obviously nothing: For these passages are obviously nothing but a bold development of Deuteronomy 32:8–9.
Foreign gods are called shedim (Deut. 32: Foreign gods are called shedim (Deut. 32:17; Ps. 106:37; cf. i Cor. 10:20), rendered "demons" or "devils" in most translations. The word is related to Akkadian šêdu ("demon"; good or evil).
Frederick Greenspahn's Encyclopedia of R: Frederick Greenspahn's Encyclopedia of Religion entry on Isaac says that, according to one version, he actually died and was then revived. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on the Akedah says a Talmudic teacher explained the ashes placed on the Ark on fast days as a reminder of the “ashes of Isaac”; that Ibn Ezra, commenting on Genesis 22:19, quotes an opinion that Abraham did kill Isaac, who was later resurrected, and rejects it as contrary to the biblical text; and that Shalom Spiegel showed such views enjoyed a wide circulation and occasionally found expression in medieval writings. Ellen Davis's Bible Odyssey article prefers the name “binding” to “sacrifice”, since Isaac was released before the sacrifice was accomplished.
Furthermore, if historical, Luke’s accou: Furthermore, if historical, Luke’s account would contradict Matthew’s clear indication that Jesus was born shortly before the death of Herod I (that is, around a decade earlier, in 6 B.C.E.). Attempts to suggest that Luke’s reference to the “first registration” (Luke 2:2) was an earlier census carried out by Quirinius have not been successful.
Gehenna appears in the New Testament 12: Gehenna appears in the New Testament 12 times, where its terrors for the wicked, as a place “where the worm never dies, and their fire is never quenched” ( Mark 9:48, quoting Isaiah 66:24), are stressed.
Gen 1 occurs over seven days, and the En: Gen 1 occurs over seven days, and the Enuma Elish is told across seven tablets. On the sixth day God creates humans, which Marduk does in the sixth tablet of the Enuma Elish.
Genesis 1 is formalized, it's highly str: Genesis 1 is formalized, it's highly structured, it has the seven days and everything's paired up. It's beautifully structured, it's very abstract. Genesis 2 is much more dramatic, much more earthy.
Genesis 1 refers to God, as in your tran: Genesis 1 refers to God, as in your translation "God," Elohim, the word that's translated as "God." He's remote, he's transcendent. He creates effortlessly through his word and through his will.
Genesis 1 speaks of male and female, one: Genesis 1 speaks of male and female, one set of Hebrew terms, but Genesis 2 uses man and woman, a different set of Hebrew terms to describe the genders.
Genesis 1, the first creation account, i: Genesis 1, the first creation account, is attributed to P.
Genesis 1:2 says that darkness was on th: Genesis 1:2 says that darkness was on the face of the deep, and the Hebrew word, tehom, has no definite article. Hayes says it is etymologically the same word as Tiamat, the feminine ending aside, and Paul's entry calls the two etymological equivalents. The NABRE's notes call the abyss the primordial ocean of ancient Semitic cosmogony, and read verse 2 as the chaos out of which God brings order. With the wind of God sweeping over the waters, Hayes argues, the storyteller sets the stage for the cosmic battle that everyone knew, and then tells no battle: the elements are there, but demythologized, and God imposes order on water that is just water. The Coogan and Chapman summary likewise gives the demythologizing of the battle before creation as an example of how Genesis transforms Near Eastern myth. Paul draws the same contrast: Tiamat is a primal generative force, while tehom is merely a poetic term for a lifeless mass of water. Hayes and Paul both note that biblical poetry elsewhere alludes to the older story of a battle with a sea monster, and that Genesis 1 pointedly leaves it out; Paul reads the mention of “the great sea monsters” in Genesis 1:21 as most likely part of that polemic.
George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam s: George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam say that in chapters 6–11 the sons of God of Genesis 6:2, identified as angels or Watchers led by their chieftain Shemihazah, mate with mortal women and beget giants who devastate the earth, and that interwoven with this is a second pair of myths in which the Watchers' sin is the revelation of forbidden secrets, with Asael as chieftain; chapters 12–16 then interpret chapters 6–11. The Harkins, Coblentz Bautch and Endres introduction describes the same two interwoven traditions, the knowledge Asael reveals including metalworking, makeup, weaponry, magic and astrology. Archie Wright says it is generally acknowledged that the Book of the Watchers combines several components that were likely separate traditions, and reports Devorah Dimant's argument for three strands. Andrei Orlov says scholars usually attribute the Shemihazah and Asael stories to two literary traditions, though some object to treating them in isolation. Miryam Brand's TheTorah.com article counts three threads, with the desire of the angels led by Shemihazah to mate with human women as the predominant one. Boling and Proctor describe the two chief angels the same way.
God’s enemies lie dead outside the walls: God’s enemies lie dead outside the walls of the New Jerusalem; just as in the past, corpses, filth and refuse lay in the Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna) outside the city; cf. 34:1–4; 2 Kgs 23:10.
Got Questions Ministries, an evangelical: Got Questions Ministries, an evangelical ministry, says the book identifies the prophet Daniel as its author and was likely written between 540 and 530 BCE; another of its pages puts it between 536 and 530 BCE, near the end of his captivity. Ligonier Ministries' Reformation Study Bible says certain details in Daniel 11:36–12:3 cannot be harmonized with the death of Antiochus IV, and that for this reason some interpreters read those verses as describing the Antichrist.
Grantley McDonald's Leiden study of the: Grantley McDonald's Leiden study of the passage says the manuscript evidence led, in the first half of the twentieth century, to the virtually universal rejection of the comma's authenticity among professional biblical critics. He says the comma is first found fully articulated in Latin creeds, that the Greek manuscript evidence before the fourteenth century is negative, and that the first Greek Bible to contain it was copied in 1362–1363. Holmes lists 1 John 5:7b–8a among the added verses. The Trinitarian Bible Society upholds the passage as inspired by God.
Hayes counts Goliath being killed twice,: Hayes counts Goliath being killed twice, once by David and once by another hero, among the duplicates scholars take as evidence that 1 Samuel combines conflicting sources, and Carol Meyers's and Keith Bodner's Bible Odyssey articles name the same tension. The Encyclopaedia Judaica and the notes of the New American Bible say the author of Chronicles resolved the contradiction by having Elhanan kill Lahmi, the brother of Goliath. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary reports that some interpreters think the oldest tradition did not name David's opponent and that the name of Elhanan's victim was later given to him. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says some scholars hold Elhanan was David's original name, but judges it more likely that Elhanan's exploit was transferred to the more famous David. The NABRE notes say 1 Samuel 16–17 holds two traditions of how David entered Saul's service, of which the Greek translation keeps only one. Sandie Gravett's Bible Odyssey article says more critical readers recognise the tale as apocryphal, and the Encyclopaedia Judaica reports Alexander Rofé's argument for a post-exilic date. Moshe Garsiel argues that, despite its legendary elements and textual problems, the general reality of the story of the duel should prevail.
Hayes says creation in Genesis 1 is not: Hayes says creation in Genesis 1 is not described as making something out of utter nothing, creation ex nihilo, but as organizing pre-existing materials and imposing order on them: when God begins, something already exists, without shape. The Coogan and Chapman summary says that in this account God does not create the universe out of nothing, and that the cosmos was formed out of untamed, though preexisting, matter; it counts the formation of the cosmos out of existing matter, in Enuma Elish Tiamat's body, among the account's affinities with the Babylonian epic. Paul's entry says the verb in the first sentence does not imply creation out of nothing, as most traditional commentators believed, but denotes, as it does throughout the Bible, a divine activity that is effortlessly effected.
Hayes's Yale lectures say the Covenant C: Hayes's Yale lectures say the Covenant Code limited the term of Israelite slavery to six years and the Priestly code prohibits it altogether, so that no Israelite can enslave another. Sweeney says Deuteronomy calls for the release of female debt slaves after six years, where the Covenant Code kept them permanently as wives, and requires creditors to supply a released slave from the wealth earned in his service; he says the Holiness Code (Leviticus 17–26) has no such thing as an Israelite slave. Farber's Bible Odyssey article says the Pentateuch has three conflicting sets of laws on the release of Hebrew slaves, with women purchased permanently as wives in Exodus 21:7–11 but treated like men in Deuteronomy 15:12. Farber also reports that several scholars think Deuteronomy improved the position of women.
He could have singled out various sins,: He could have singled out various sins, but he chose to take same-sex relations as his example (Rom 1:24-28). It represented both to him and to his readers pagan depravity.
He forms the human like a potter working: He forms the human like a potter working with clay. He talks to himself, he plants a garden, he takes a stroll in the garden in the cool of the evening. He makes clothes for Adam and Eve. He's spoken of in much more anthropomorphic terms then the God that we encounter in Genesis 1.

Holmes says Erasmus had only a very smal: Holmes says Erasmus had only a very small number of Greek manuscripts, the ones he used most from the twelfth century and the oldest, which he used least, from the tenth.
