Max Botner's Bible Odyssey article says many specialists date some form of the Parables before the Synoptic Gospels.
Lucifer (Lat., ‘light-bringer’). In the: Lucifer (Lat., ‘light-bringer’). In the Vulgate and Authorized Version of Isaiah 14. 12 (‘How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer’), an epithet for the king of Babylon. By some of the fathers it was taken in conjunction with Luke 10. 18 as a name for the devil, so that the whole passage Isaiah 14. 12–16 became one basis for the myth (developed in Milton's Paradise Lost) that the devil is a rebellious angel cast into hell.
Luke sets the parousia at a later date,: Luke sets the parousia at a later date, after “the time of the Gentiles” ( Lk 21:24 ).
Lv 20:10 and Dt 22:22 portray adultery a: Lv 20:10 and Dt 22:22 portray adultery as a capital crime. The death penalty was to be meted out to both the woman and the man involved in the act. Contemporary scholarship shows that there is considerable debate about this punishment. Some scholars consider that the death penalty was "on the books" but that actual practice was somewhat different. Hos 2:4 and later rabbinic texts suggest that divorce was a penalty actually incurred by an adulterous woman.
Lynn Huber's Bible Odyssey article names: Lynn Huber's Bible Odyssey article names Genesis 19:1–11, Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, Romans 1:26–28, 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 and 1 Timothy 1:9–10 as a collection of passages commonly called the “clobber passages”. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the most explicit Old Testament references are in the Holiness Code of Leviticus, and that the New Testament contains three references to homosexual practice, two of them in lists of vices. William Loader's Bible Odyssey article says there are very few references in the New Testament, all in writings associated with Paul.
Many contemporary scholars now reject We: Many contemporary scholars now reject Wellhausen’s claims that Exodus 34 contains an ancient Ritual Decalogue with later expansions and argue instead that it, as a whole, represents a late compilation that draws on earlier laws.
Many dates have been suggested for the f: Many dates have been suggested for the first version of Genesis 37–50, which range from the beginning of the first millennium bce (or even earlier) until the Hellenistic Period.
Many people are most surprised to learn: Many people are most surprised to learn that nowhere in the Bible is Mary Magdalene described as a prostitute. Her reputation as a reformed prostitute has no explicit biblical support, but it does have church support. Pope Gregory I (d. 604) gave legs to this misinterpretation by delivering a sermon that equated both Mary of Bethany and the anonymous hair-washing sinner woman (Luke 7:36-50) with Mary Magdalene.
Many scholars have suggested that two of: Many scholars have suggested that two of the Pentateuch's sources, P and E, preserve a memory of a time when Israel worshipped the Canaanite god El. Christine Hayes's Yale lecture points to Exodus 6:2–4, assigned to P, where God tells Moses that he appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as El Shaddai but did not make himself known to them by his name Yahweh. The J source, by contrast, has the earliest humans worship Yahweh by name from Genesis 4:26. The patriarchs, Hayes says, seem to have worshipped El, and P and E insist that they worshipped God as El and that God revealed himself as Yahweh at the time of the Exodus. The chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's introductory textbook likewise says Genesis appears to preserve a tradition from the period when Israel's ancestors prayed to El, the Canaanite god worshipped by Israel's neighbors. Its summary of the Exodus chapter notes that the sources all present the God of the ancestors and the God of the Exodus as continuous, but reads God's first revealing himself as Yahweh in Exodus as an echo of change, recalling a time when the Israelites switched their loyalties from the worship of the sky god to the worship of the storm-god.
Marius Nel counts eight copies of the bi: Marius Nel counts eight copies of the biblical book among the Qumran scrolls, and Craig Evans eight fragmentary scrolls. Nel dates 4QDanc to the late second or early first century BCE, closer to its original than any other biblical book among the scrolls. Popović and colleagues' 2025 radiocarbon test gives 4Q114, a copy of Daniel 8–11, a range of 230–160 BCE, which they say makes it one of the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of its presumed authors. Nel notes that the scrolls preserve the shift from Hebrew to Aramaic at 2:4b and back to Hebrew at 8:1.
Marriage itself was a social arrangement: Marriage itself was a social arrangement wherein women were exchanged, that is, given over for some monetary or property return by fathers (Gn 29.14b–30) or brothers (Gn 24.29–54).
Marriage was typically conducted when an: Marriage was typically conducted when an unmarried woman, living in her father’s house, was transferred into her husband’s jurisdiction by his payment of the “bride price” to her father (Gen 34:12).
Mary Magdalene, or “of Magdala,” mention: Mary Magdalene, or “of Magdala,” mentioned first in every listing of Jesus’s female disciples (Matt 27:55-56; Matt 27:61; Matt 28:1; Mark 15:40-41; Mark 15:47; Mark 16:1; Luke 8:2-3; Luke 24:10). She seems to have been the leader of a group of women who “followed” and “served” Jesus constantly from the outset of his ministry in Galilee and who provided for Jesus’s ministry from their own means (Luke 8:1-3).
Mary, the mother of James, or of James a: Mary, the mother of James, or of James and Joses, or Joseph, or “the other Mary,” among the women disciples at the cross (Matt 27:55-56; Mark 15:40), with Mary Magdalene at the burial, empty tomb (Matt 27:61; Matt 28:1; Mark 15:47; Mark 16:1), and first appearance of the risen Christ (Matt 28:9).
Megan Warner's Bible Odyssey article say: Megan Warner's Bible Odyssey article says scholarly views about Genesis 2:24 vary greatly: all agree that it is an etiology, a text that explains something, and most that an editor added it later than the primary author of Genesis 2, but some scholars think it functions as a normative definition of marriage, though the word marriage appears nowhere in the text, while others argue that it does not intend to provide one, that it describes what does happen rather than what must happen; readers, she says, have long used it as a lens on divorce and polygamy. Lutz Doering writes that the form of the verse quoted in Mark 10, with the added words “and the two shall become one flesh”, represents a tradition of interpretation that apparently reflects a tendency in Second Temple Judaism to prefer monogamy to polygamy. Paul Heger writes that even with “the two” the verse does not absolutely convey a divine prohibition of polygamy, and that the Qumran writers drew their prohibition of polygamy not from this verse but from Genesis 1:27.
Meghan Henning's Bible Odyssey article s: Meghan Henning's Bible Odyssey article says Paul's letters make no explicit mention of eternal punishment or hell: Paul speaks of the coming day of judgment and wrath, but warns of the consequences of sin rather than describing a place of eternal punishment. Carol Bakhos's introduction in the Posen Library says Paul describes the wicked as simply being destroyed, with no mention of any kind of hell. Hanré Janse van Rensburg and Ernest van Eck's article in HTS Teologiese Studies, following Alan Bernstein, says Paul never used the word Gehenna, and that the one place he refers to Hades, 1 Corinthians 15:54–55, celebrates the defeat of death, and that Paul in effect adopted annihilation.
Michael Holmes's Bible Odyssey article s: Michael Holmes's Bible Odyssey article says the KJV's translators used a printed Greek text that included about 16 verses not in more recent printed editions, and that older manuscript evidence made it clear the text had “grown” slightly as it was copied by hand. He lists them: Matthew 17:21, 18:11 and 23:14, Mark 7:16, 9:44, 9:46, 11:26 and 15:28, Luke 17:36 and 23:17, John 5:3b–4, Acts 8:37, 15:34 and 24:6b–8a, Romans 16:24 and 1 John 5:7b–8a. He says only the few modern translations that use the KJV's Greek text, such as the New King James Version, still include them, while others, such as the NASB, put them in brackets with a footnote. The notes of the New American Bible, Revised Edition, say Matthew 17:21 is added in some manuscripts, that Mark 9:44 and 9:46 are lacking in some important early manuscripts and are omitted as scribal additions, that John 5:4 is missing from all early Greek manuscripts, and that the oldest and best manuscripts of Acts omit 8:37. Tommy Wasserman's Bible Odyssey article says the doxology at the end of the Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6:13 is lacking in the most ancient manuscripts and that textual scholars think it was added later. Holmes's list leaves out the two longer passages, Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11, treated below.
Michael Peppard's Bible Odyssey article: Michael Peppard's Bible Odyssey article says Matthew 28:19 is the only biblical passage that connects baptism with the invocation of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen sees a definite shift from binitarianism to trinitarianism in the New Testament, while saying that nowhere in it are the relations among Father, Son and Spirit clarified in any systematic manner. Jack Levison's St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology entry describes a more historical mode of reading for which the few possible glimpses of the Trinity in the New Testament, such as Matthew 28:16–20, are not substantial enough to claim a well-developed trinitarian view of the spirit there.
More critical readers recognize the apoc: More critical readers recognize the apocryphal nature of this tale. Not only is it one of two accounts of how David came into the service of Saul (the other being as a musician, 1Sam 16:18-23), it also conflicts with 2Sam 21:19, which states that a fighter named Elhanan defeated Goliath in a different battle.
Moses’s retelling, however, makes one si: Moses’s retelling, however, makes one significant revision: the Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy makes no mention of God’s work of creation as found in the Exodus version. Instead, Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath commandment in the experience of Israelite slavery in Egypt (Deut 5:15).
Most Christian Zionists hold dispensatio: Most Christian Zionists hold dispensationalist views that normally include beliefs about a literal future millennial reign of peace (Rv 20:1–6) from the current Jerusalem, the rebuilding of the temple and the reinstatement of the Old Testament sacrificial system.
Most scholars agree that they would have: Most scholars agree that they would have understood them to refer to the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem as God’s judgment upon Israel. However, they would see the Son of Man as the risen Jesus of Nazareth coming from heaven in glory, as in 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17, and they anticipated him imminently (Stein 2014, 112–17).
Neighboring cultures believed that the d: Neighboring cultures believed that the dead lived on in the underworld in a communicative state (Deut 18:9-14), but Israel’s theologians taught that they were, for practical purposes, nonexistent (Eccl 9:5-6). Nonetheless, foreign ideas and practices continued (1Sam 28; Isa 8:19).
Nephilim (literally “fallen ones”) are f: Nephilim (literally “fallen ones”) are first mentioned in Gen 6:1–4, a famously difficult passage that tells of an apparent breach in the boundary between the divine and the human realms in primordial times.
Nevertheless, the law as formulated in D: Nevertheless, the law as formulated in Deuteronomy 22:22 singles out the married woman who has been possessed by her husband, and demands of her an uncompromising sexual exclusivity, which admits no exception or extenuating circumstances. Thus, any intercourse between a married woman and man other than her husband is taken to constitute adultery, whether the woman was a consenting partner or not.
Nevertheless, there are passages where d: Nevertheless, there are passages where demon-like creatures may be implied (see Isa 34:14–15) or where foreign gods may carry demonic valences (see Deut 32:17).
No god but me: with Second Isaiah, Israe: No god but me: with Second Isaiah, Israel’s faith is declared to be explicitly monotheistic. However implicit it may have been, earlier formulas did not exclude the existence of other gods, not even that of the first commandment: “You shall not have other gods besides me” (Ex 20:3).
No scholar doubts this event: not only i: No scholar doubts this event: not only is the story found in both Mark and John but the embarrassment felt by the Gospel writers regarding the obvious conundrum of a sinless Jesus’ baptism for the forgiveness of sin (see especially Matt 3:14-15) suggests a long-established tradition.
No wonder that most scholars who dealt w: No wonder that most scholars who dealt with the early history of Israel avoided using the account of 2 Sam 8:1–14 for their historical reconstruction and treated it as late historiographical work that does not reflect the ancient reality.
Nor does it mention Paul by name: instea: Nor does it mention Paul by name: instead, it confronts the challenge he presents—most seriously in his law-free gospel that emphasizes faith in a way that seems to ignore works, hearing, and believing without doing (Jas 1:22-25, Jas 2:14-26).
Nuria Calduch-Benages's Bible Odyssey ar: Nuria Calduch-Benages's Bible Odyssey article says that although it is not known how frequent polygamy was in ancient Israel, the Deuteronomic legislation assumes it, setting out whose offspring would inherit (Deuteronomy 21:15–17) and advising kings against it (Deuteronomy 17:17), and that while most first marriages in the biblical accounts are monogamous, there are many famous polygamous men, among them Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon. Tracy Lemos's Bible Odyssey article says men could have multiple wives and concubines, so that monogamy was a one-way street, and that it is hard to know how common polygamy really was. Solomon O. Ademiluka writes that the Old Testament presents a culture in which polygamy was practised largely unchallenged, and that it is generally accepted amongst scholars that the Old Testament is not opposed to it. Isaac Sassoon writes that the texts, in the main, condone polygyny, “but not downright”, and that polygyny, though pervasive, need not have been ubiquitous. Sarah Malena's Bible Odyssey article says the author of 1 Kings 11:1–3 claims that Solomon had 700 wives and 300 concubines, and that Solomon followed the model of ancient Near Eastern kingship, which proved contrary to values that would become biblical theological foundations (Deuteronomy 17; 1 Samuel 8). The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says that although polygamous marriages are known in the Bible, monogamous marriage clearly became the ideal and normative expectation.
Omer Sergi’s “Saul, David, and the Forma: Omer Sergi’s “Saul, David, and the Formation of the Israelite Monarchy: Revisiting the Historical and Literary Context of 1 Samuel 9–2 Samuel 5” contests one of the most accepted hypotheses in biblical scholarship, namely, that the biblical traditions about Saul originated in the kingdom of Israel and that they arrived in Judah only after the fall of Samaria (720 BCE) and stimulated the composition of the stories about David’s rise, which are dated, accordingly, to the seventh century BCE.
On a larger scale, the book of Joshua pr: On a larger scale, the book of Joshua proclaims that the Israelites conquered “the whole land” (e.g., Josh 10:40), but the book of Judges describes the survival of many Canaanites and other peoples.
On the whole, then, Paul's description o: On the whole, then, Paul's description of the Parousia in 1 Thess 4:15-17 comes closer to what we know of Hellenistic formal receptions than Cosby allows.
Once the account in Exodus 34 is decoupl: Once the account in Exodus 34 is decoupled from the other accounts, it becomes clear that the Ten Words in 34:28 is almost certainly not a reference to the Decalogue of Exodus 20. Rather, these Ten Words much more naturally refer to the cultic laws listed in verses 10-26 of this very chapter.
One thing that most people do in fact ag: One thing that most people do in fact agree on is that the oldest account of the event is a poetic fragment that's found in Exodus 15, verses one to 12, in particular.
Only one angel is said to be able to fly: Only one angel is said to be able to fly (Dn 9.21).
Or in 1Sam 17:50, David kills Goliath, w: Or in 1Sam 17:50, David kills Goliath, whereas in 2Sam 21:19, Elhanan does.
Other biblical descriptions of God are m: Other biblical descriptions of God are much more reminiscent of the Canaanite storm-god Baal, who in Canaanite mythology defeated El and took his place as head of the pantheon. Like Baal, Yahweh is said to ride on the clouds, his revelations come with thunderstorms and earthquakes, and poetic fragments allude to his victory over water foes. In the Song of the Sea in Exodus 15, Yahweh is described as a storm-god. Hayes reports Michael Coogan's observation that Baal was the key figure in a change in the religion of Canaan somewhere between 1500 and 1200 BCE, part of a wider pattern in which a younger storm-god takes power from an older god by defeating a water god. Following Coogan, she finds that in Exodus 15 there seems to be a collective memory of a similar change in Israel's religion, in which Yahweh establishes himself as the god of the Israelites in place of El. The chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's textbook describes a fundamental shift by the end of the Late Bronze Age, in which a younger god, usually identified as a storm-god, supplants an older one.
Other differences include the duration o: Other differences include the duration of the flood (“40 days” in Gen 7:17; “150 days” in Gen 7:24), the number of each animal entering the ark (“two of each” in Gen 6:19; “seven pairs of clean” and “one pair of unclean” in Gen 7:2), and the types of birds sent to determine if dry land has appeared (“a raven” in Gen 8:7; “a dove” three times in Gen 8:8-12).
Other scholars disagree, arguing either: Other scholars disagree, arguing either that Gen 2:24 has nothing to do with marriage at all or, if it is an etiology about marriage, that it does not intend to provide a normative definition of marriage. In other words, Gen 2:24 is a descriptive explanation (this is what does happen) rather than normative explanation (this is what must happen.)
Other terms—like arsenkoitai and malakoi: Other terms—like arsenkoitai and malakoi in 1Cor 6:9 or para phusin in Rom 1:26–27—seem to refer to specific sexual practices or preferences, but scholars disagree on exactly what those are.
Overall, married men in ancient Israel h: Overall, married men in ancient Israel had greater sexual freedom than married women, since they could have sex with unpledged virgins (Deut 22.28-29) and prostitutes (Judges 16.1) with a penalty less than death applied.
Part of it, “the upper water” (Ps 148:4;: Part of it, “the upper water” (Ps 148:4; Dn 3:60), is held up by the dome of the sky (vv. 6–7), from which rain descends on the earth
Paul Heger writes that the rabbis and mo: Paul Heger writes that the rabbis and most translators and commentators, including the Septuagint, understood the “sister” of Leviticus 18:18 as a real sister, so that the verse forbids marriage with two sisters during their lifetimes, which he calls the common interpretation; he reports Mayer Gruber's contrary view that the verse explicitly and clearly prohibits polygamy, and argues against it. Isaac Sassoon writes that Leviticus 18:18 is cryptic, hence the dispute over whether it bans polygyny, as the Damascus Document took it, or marriage to a woman and her biological sister, and that scholars, Angelo Tosato among them, have reopened the case; his own study brought him close to Tosato's position, from the phrase “a woman to her sister”, which in all eight of its other uses signifies a relationship between two objects, never two people. Sassoon writes that the Damascus Document's phrase “by taking two wives in their lives” unmistakably echoes Leviticus 18:18; Heger argues that the resemblance does not show that Leviticus 18:18 is the source of its prohibition.
Paul is the first writer in Greek litera: Paul is the first writer in Greek literature to employ this term (see also 1 Tim 1:10), which makes it especially challenging to translate.
Paul mentions “male-bedders” and “softie: Paul mentions “male-bedders” and “softies,” probably referring to active and passive male partners (1Cor 6:9-10; see also 1Tim 1:10).
Paul never used the word Gehenna, and in: Paul never used the word Gehenna, and in the one place he refers to Hades it is in the context of celebrating the resurrection of the flesh and the defeat of death (1 Cor 15:54-55).
Paul's teaching on divorce and remarriag: Paul's teaching on divorce and remarriage in 1 Corinthians 7 is regarded as so problematic that there is still a debate about whether or not it contains any teaching on remarriage at all.
Paul’s concern is not just pederasty but: Paul’s concern is not just pederasty but also consensual sex (Rom 1:27).
Persian Dualism may have been influentia: Persian Dualism may have been influential but there is no evidence that the Chronicler felt the need to remove all aspects of evil from originating in God. Although not representing a complete doctrine of Satan, as developed in later Jewish writings, 1 Chronicles 21 is an important stage its development.
Pieter Craffert's article in HTS Teologi: Pieter Craffert's article in HTS Teologiese Studies says the one aspect most historical Jesus scholars agree on is that Jesus was a successful healer and an exorcist of repute, but that there is no agreement on what he did when exorcising demons. Graham Twelftree's Bible Odyssey article says Mark portrays Jesus as a prolific exorcist, that no other figure in antiquity is known for whom exorcism was so important, and that John's Gospel mentions no exorcisms. Travis Proctor's Bible Odyssey article says exorcism is the miracle of Jesus that Mark mentions most often, that Mark's first miracle is an exorcism in the synagogue at Capernaum (Mark 1:21–28), and that the idea that demons could possess bodies and be cast out by ritual experts is found in Jewish texts such as the Dead Sea Scrolls and Josephus.
Pope Gregory I (d. 604) gave legs to thi: Pope Gregory I (d. 604) gave legs to this misinterpretation by delivering a sermon that equated both Mary of Bethany and the anonymous hair-washing sinner woman (Luke 7:36-50) with Mary Magdalene.
R. F. Collins's New Catholic Encyclopedi: R. F. Collins's New Catholic Encyclopedia article says Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 make adultery a capital crime for both the woman and the man, that contemporary scholarship shows considerable debate about this punishment, some scholars considering that the death penalty was “on the books” but that actual practice was somewhat different, and that Hosea 2:4 and later rabbinic texts suggest divorce was the penalty an adulterous woman actually incurred. Cynthia Edenburg writes that Deuteronomy 22:22 dropped the clause in cuneiform law that let the husband set the penalty, even though other biblical sources imply that spousal discretion was respected in practice. William Loader writes that by at least the first century CE Jews no longer had the right to execute offenders, and that where the death penalty was not enacted divorce was the obvious alternative and was mandatory. Deborah Rooke notes that Numbers 5:11–31 lets a man who suspects his wife of adultery make her undergo an ordeal before the priest, and that no such ordeal exists for men; Ishay Rosen-Zvi writes that there are no accounts from biblical times of the ritual being performed, and that it was probably discontinued, if it was ever practised, during the Second Temple era.
References to עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים in Deut: References to עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים in Deuteronomy’s retelling of the theophany at Sinai/Horeb, however (4:13, 10:4), seem to understand the laws spoken by YHWH as the better-known Decalogue of Deuteronomy 5 (= Exodus 20).
Reyburn and Fry's UBS handbook on Genesi: Reyburn and Fry's UBS handbook on Genesis says the meaning of bene ʾelohim has been greatly disputed, that as a Hebrew idiom it means beings who belong to the class of “gods”, and that nearly all translations take it as some kind of heavenly beings; it also reports ancient Jewish authorities who read it as aristocrats and interpreters who read it as the descendants of Cain and Seth. The New American Bible's notes call the sons of God other heavenly beings. Rachel Adelman's and Michael Segal's TheTorah.com articles say the phrase always refers to divine or angelic beings elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, and Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article lists Genesis 6:2 among the texts that call heavenly beings “gods”. Jaap Doedens's dissertation says the divine-beings interpretation has been the majority view since the beginning of the twentieth century, and that the angels interpretation is the earliest known. He says Julius Africanus is the first church writer known to have read the sons of God as Sethites, a reading that became dominant among the church fathers from the fourth century, and that the Targumim prefer a non-supernatural reading such as “mighty ones”; Adelman says some rabbis read elohim as judges or lords. E. O. Usue's article in Verbum et Ecclesia finds basically no consensus among scholars and adopts the reading kings or rulers.
Satan's evil function in 1 Chr 21.1, the: Satan's evil function in 1 Chr 21.1, then, shows that the Chronicler was aware of a personal principle of evil that warred against God and enticed man to rebel against Him.
Scholarly views about the meaning of Gen: Scholarly views about the meaning of Gen 2:24 vary greatly. One thing that all agree on is that Gen 2:24 is an etiology, a text that explains something. Most scholars also agree that Gen 2:24 was added by an editor working later than the primary author of Gen 2, perhaps to address the needs of a later audience. What is it that Gen 2:24 explains? This is where scholarly opinion begins to diverge.
Scholars also debate about the kind of s: Scholars also debate about the kind of sexual practice that Paul is referring to in 1Cor 6:9-10. Some have argued it is primarily pederasty (a homosexual relationship between a grown man, often married, and an adolescent boy) and that Paul would not have known about our concept of sexual orientation. Others disagree and say that Paul’s statements do indeed categorize all homosexual behavior as “unrighteous.”
Scholars disagree as to whether the even: Scholars disagree as to whether the events described in Ruth 4 relate to the institution of levirate marriage (also known simply as “levirate”).
Scholars have long explored the relation: Scholars have long explored the relationship of the tradition described in 1 En. 6–11 to the tradition in Gen. 6:1-4, though there is no absolute consensus as to how that relationship might be named. In the last fifty years, scholars have tended to favor the idea that the Book of the Watchers depends on the account in Gen. 6:1-4; still, some prominent dissidents have argued that Genesis features an abbreviated account of the Enochic version. Recently a growing number of voices have suggested that both Genesis and the Book of the Watchers feature independent renderings of a common tradition
Scholars note a tension between this sto: Scholars note a tension between this story (1Sam 17) and the one in 2Sam 21:19-22, which reports that a certain Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath.
Schrader points out that Martha was abse: Schrader points out that Martha was absent from John 11:1–3 in P66 before it was corrected.
Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey article: Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey article says 1 Samuel 28, where a necromancer calls up the dead Samuel, suggests that Israelites believed in some sort of continued existence, that grave goods and tomb installations in Iron Age Judah show the dead were fed and sustained by the living, and that the evidence shows a widespread belief in a dark and shadowy existence after death. Matthew Suriano's article in the Journal of Hebrew Scriptures says the presence of grave goods indicates a belief in Iron Age Judah that the dead continued to exist inside the tomb, and notes that an earlier generation of scholars, such as Johannes Pedersen, concluded the Israelites lacked any positive notion of existence after death. Kerry Sonia's book on caring for the dead in ancient Israel says the subject divides scholarly opinion: she argues that the cult of dead kin did exist, and reports a minimalist reading, which she cites to Brian Schmidt and Philip Johnston, that the lack of explicit reference to it in the Hebrew Bible indicates its absence. The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says Israel's theologians taught that the dead were, for practical purposes, nonexistent, though foreign ideas and practices continued.

Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey article says that although Jewish tradition translates Deuteronomy 6:4 as “YHWH our God, YHWH is One”, the Hebrew is fairly ambiguous and could equally be rendered “YHWH is our god, YHWH alone”, which would reflect a monolatrous belief; she adds that in the preexilic world in which much of Deuteronomy was composed, the idea of monotheism had not fully emerged. Jeffrey Tigay's commentary on Deuteronomy lists three possible renderings and judges “YHVH is our God, YHVH alone” the most likely, though not certain, noting that the chapter is concerned with Israel's relationship to God, not with his nature. Reuven Kimelman writes that the ancient Israelites likely saw the verse originally as a declaration of monolatry. The New American Bible's note gives other possible translations, and reads the passage as saying that the Lord alone is God. Dolansky writes that some Jews in the Second Temple period began to develop the idea that YHWH was the only God and reinterpreted their earlier texts in this light, as the Septuagint's “YHWH is one” shows. Louis Jacobs's Encyclopaedia Judaica entry calls the Shema the supreme affirmation in Jewish thought of the unity of God.

Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey article says the Hebrew Bible never describes a fiery place of eternal torment for sinners, and that Sheol holds all of the dead without judgment or torment. Meghan Henning's Bible Odyssey article says Sheol, the Pit and Abaddon can all name a space that holds all of the dead, righteous and unrighteous, with no torment for the dead there. Carol Bakhos's introduction in the Posen Library says the notion that the wicked will be eternally tormented in hell does not appear in the Hebrew Bible. Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say Sheol is an ancient Israelite notion of a shadowy place beneath the soil, not connected with reward or punishment after death. Shaul Shaked's entry in the Encyclopaedia Iranica, setting out the case for Zoroastrian influence, says there was no notion of heaven and hell up to the end of the Old Testament period. The UBS translators' handbook on Genesis says Sheol was regarded as a dark and gloomy place where all the dead were, and should not be translated by a word for “hell”, a place of punishment. The New American Bible's note on Psalm 6 calls Sheol the underworld where the souls of the dead dwelt, similar to the Greek Hades. Matthew Suriano's article in the Journal of Hebrew Scriptures adds that Sheol was not the sum of all burials but a metaphor for the marginalizing experience of dying, an intermediary stage every person endured in death.
She is also described as one “from whom: She is also described as one “from whom seven demons had gone out” (Luke 8:2), indicating that she had been healed of some serious affliction. She is featured foremost as a witness to Jesus’s death (Matt 27:55-56; Matt 27:61; Mark 15:40-41; Mark 15:47; Luke 23:49; Luke 23:55-56, John 19:25) and to the empty tomb (Matt 28:1; Matt 28:6; Mark 16:1-6; Luke 24:1-3; Luke 24:10; John 20:1-2).
She is commissioned to announce the news: She is commissioned to announce the news of Christ's resurrection to the disciples (Matt 28:5-9; Mark 16:6-7; Luke 24:4-10).
Sheol is a place that holds all of the d: Sheol is a place that holds all of the dead (see Gen 37:35; 1Sam 2:6; Isa 28:15) without judgment or torment.
Sheol, the Pit, and Abaddon can all be u: Sheol, the Pit, and Abaddon can all be used to talk about a space that holds all of the dead, both the righteous and unrighteous (see, for instance, Gen 37:35; 1Sam 2:6; Isa 28:15). They are dusty, dark, and undesirable spaces to go, but there is not any kind of torment for the dead there.
So Israelite accounts of creation contai: So Israelite accounts of creation contain clear allusions to and resonances of Ancient Near Eastern cosmogonies; but perhaps Genesis 1 can best be described as demythologizing what was a common cultural heritage.
So creation in Genesis 1 is not describe: So creation in Genesis 1 is not described as a process of making something out of nothing: that's a notion referred to as creation ex nihilo, creation of something out of utter nothing. It's instead a process of organizing pre-existing materials and imposing order on those chaotic materials.
So in Genesis 2 the deity is Yahweh Eloh: So in Genesis 2 the deity is Yahweh Elohim.
So in the second creation story beginnin: So in the second creation story beginning in Genesis 2:4, we read that the first human is formed when God fashions it from the dust of the earth or clay.
So the main characteristics of the J sou: So the main characteristics of the J source, which begins with the second creation story, so the J source picks up in Genesis 2:4, second half of verse 4 are
So what we have in the first few chapter: So what we have in the first few chapters of Genesis are two creation stories that have distinctive styles, distinctive themes, distinctive vocabularies and they're placed side by side. In Genesis 6 through 9 we seem to have two flood stories with distinctive styles, and themes, and vocabularies, and substantive details, but they're interwoven instead of being placed side by side.
So you have this firmament, which is bea: So you have this firmament, which is beaten back to hold back primeval waters that are pressing in; you have land which is holding down the waters here. We inhabit the bubble that's created in that way. That's the image in Enuma Elish and it's the image of Genesis 1.
So you've got some people reading Romans: So you've got some people reading Romans 1 as a condemnation of modern homosexuality and thinking they're doing a good historical reading of this text. You've got other people who read the same text, using the same methods of historical criticism, and say, are you crazy? He's not talking about homosexuality, that's not his concern.
Solomon followed the model for ancient N: Solomon followed the model for ancient Near Eastern kingship, but it proved contrary to values that would become biblical theological foundations (see Deut 17 and 1Sam 8).
Some manuscripts add, “But this kind doe: Some manuscripts add, “But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting”; this is a variant of the better reading of Mk 9:29.
Some of the latest written texts of the: Some of the latest written texts of the Hebrew Bible start using names for angels, such as Gabriel (Dan 8:16, Dan 9:21) and Michael (Dan 10:13).
Some scholars argue for a solely Jewish: Some scholars argue for a solely Jewish background, with the Sinai theophany or ‘coming of God’ traditions serving as the model (particularly Exodus 19:10–18; Dupont 1952, 68–69).
Some scholars have said that all looks l: Some scholars have said that all looks like those verses that teach the subordination of women in I Corinthians 14 were not originally by Paul but were a later scribal interpolation, insertion into the text. Other scholars disagree with that, and they think that these verses were original with I Corinthians 14.
Some scholars think that Gen 2:24 functi: Some scholars think that Gen 2:24 functions as a normative definition of marriage—though it should also be noted that the word marriage appears nowhere in the text.
Special rules applied to brothers living: Special rules applied to brothers living on an undivided estate. For example, Deut 25:5-10 stipulates that if one brother married but died childless, another brother was to marry the widow and hope to impregnate her with a baby boy, who would then inherit the share that the deceased had been entitled to.
Sperling's Encyclopedia of Religion entr: Sperling's Encyclopedia of Religion entry says the term elohim appears some 2,600 times in the Hebrew scriptures and, although plural in form, is often construed with a singular verb. John Barclay Burns, reviewing Joel Burnett's study of the word, calls it morphologically plural and routinely construed with a singular verb, and Hayes's lectures say that used with a singular verb it refers to the God of Israel. Sperling adds that even when Elohim refers to the God of Israel it can be treated as a plural, as in Genesis 20:13; that its plural uses most often refer to gods whose worship the biblical authors condemn; and that the singular sense is used even for illicit divinities such as Astarte, Milcom and Chemosh. Thomas Overholt's entry on the medium of Endor says she refers to Samuel's ghost as a “god” (1 Samuel 28:13), and Benjamin Cox and Susan Ackerman write that the word can refer to deceased spirits. Burns reports Burnett's argument that ilanu, a plural form that in earlier Canaanite usage was interchangeable with the singular ilu, carried the further connotation of an abstract plural, and Burnett's novel interpretation of elohim as denoting Yahweh and his divine entourage.
Stephen Cook's Bible Odyssey article say: Stephen Cook's Bible Odyssey article says the word teraphim appears fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, and that the texts show human-shaped figurines of varying sizes: those Rachel hides in Genesis 31 fit in a saddlebag, so they were smaller than the one Michal puts in David's bed in 1 Samuel 19, which the New American Bible's note calls a life-sized image of a household god in human form. Kerry Sonia writes that by far the most pervasive aspect of the teraphim in the Hebrew Bible is their association with divination, and Cook and the New American Bible's notes also link them with divination. Sonia says most scholarly treatments read them as figurines of either household gods or ancestors; the household-gods reading once dominated but seems to have largely fallen out of favour, while over the past twenty years the reading as ancestor figurines used in necromancy has gained some acceptance. Cook, and Benjamin Cox and Susan Ackerman, hold the ancestor reading; Sonia herself is unconvinced, and finds only that they were objects used in divination relatively clear. The texts also differ on whether the teraphim are acceptable: Cook notes that several, such as 1 Samuel 19:13, have no problem with them, while the New American Bible's note says that elsewhere in the Deuteronomistic History their use is condemned (1 Samuel 15:23; 2 Kings 23:24).
Strikingly, the term עשרת הדברים “The Te: Strikingly, the term עשרת הדברים “The Ten Sayings” is absent from Exodus 20!
Surprisingly, Jesus appeals to the story: Surprisingly, Jesus appeals to the story of creation, which states that “God made them male and female,” to prohibit divorce (Mark 10:3–9; see Gen 1:27).
Sydney Tooth says 1 Thessalonians 4:13–1: Sydney Tooth says 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 is the letter's fullest description of Jesus's coming: he will descend from heaven with trumpets and archangels' shouts, the dead will be raised, and the living and the raised together will ascend to be with him in the air. Tooth says there is significant debate over the origins of the imagery and its implications. Some scholars argue for a Jewish background in the Sinai theophany and coming-of-God traditions; many argue strongly for a Hellenistic background in formal receptions, when a city's residents went out to meet a visiting emperor or dignitary and accompanied him back, so that on this reading believers meet Jesus as a welcoming committee and accompany him back to earth. Robert Gundry, in the Bulletin for Biblical Research, argues that Paul's description comes closer to these receptions than Michael Cosby allows; Cosby had argued that the Greek word for “meeting” was not a technical term and that the main elements of such receptions are missing from the passage. Joseph Plevnik, in Biblica, argues that the passage depicts the bringing in of the faithful, who do not return to the earth but stay with the Lord, and that Paul's source of inspiration was Jewish rather than Hellenistic. Dale Martin's Yale lectures read Paul as saying that believers meet Jesus in the air and then all come back down to have the Kingdom of God.
Sydney Tooth says that, despite having l: Sydney Tooth says that, despite having little support among most scholars, rapture theology remains extremely popular among many Christians, and that besides 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 it draws on Matthew 24 and Revelation 20:1–6, Matthew 24:40–41 above all. The New Catholic Encyclopedia says many scholars criticize the doctrine on both biblical and theological grounds. The New American Bible notes call it a construction that combines 1 Thessalonians 4:17 with Matthew 24:40–41, Luke 17:34–35 and passages from Revelation in a scheme of millennial dispensationalism, and read the one “taken” in Matthew 24:40–41 as probably taken into the kingdom at the coming of the Son of Man. Sean Durbin says dispensationalists developed the doctrine to maintain their distinction between Israel and the church; Peter Lee's doctoral thesis on Darby says that for Darby the pretribulation rapture was derived not from Scripture as such but from the doctrine of the two peoples of God.
T. L. Fallon's entry in the New Catholic: T. L. Fallon's entry in the New Catholic Encyclopedia says the phrase “messenger of the Lord” has a more specific meaning that has not yet been satisfactorily explained: in early texts such as Genesis 16, Exodus 3 and Judges 6 the messenger is presented as God appearing to humans in sensible form. It sets out three theories (the messenger represents God; the messenger is God himself in human form; the messenger was interpolated into older stories of God appearing directly) and says each has valid elements but none solves all the problems. Stephen White's article in the Tyndale Bulletin says it is surprising how little in the literature satisfactorily explains the interchange of the angel and Yahweh, and describes the interpolation theory, which holds that “the angel of the LORD” was added where God's actions seemed too anthropomorphic. Bernard Bamberger's entry in the Encyclopaedia Judaica reports both that some scholars take the angel as a manifestation of the divine power and will and that others suppose later scribes interposed an angel where the earliest stories had God meet a human directly. Benjamin Sommer's Bible Odyssey article reads this mal'akh as a small-scale manifestation of God, part of the deity rather than a separate being.
Teraphim: a life-sized image of a househ: Teraphim: a life-sized image of a household god in human form; cf. also note on Gn 31:19.
The Apostle Paul relays Jesus’s strict c: The Apostle Paul relays Jesus’s strict command not to divorce, but, should divorce happen, he states that one should remain single or be reconciled to the former partner (1 Cor 7:10–11). Paul judges divorce permissible when a nonbelieving spouse is insistent, but a believing spouse is not to initiate a divorce (1 Cor 7:12–16).
The Book of Daniel identifies the Prophe: The Book of Daniel identifies the Prophet Daniel as its author (Daniel 9:2; 10:2).
The Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic a: The Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements says the thousand years of Revelation 20 have been understood as a precise timeframe or as an indeterminate but lengthy period, and defines premillennialism as the expectation of a Second Coming before the thousand-year reign and postmillennialism as a Second Coming after a given period of time. Charles Lippy's entry in Contemporary American Religion says premillennialism holds that Christ will return and reign over the earth for a thousand years after a time of great tribulation, that postmillennialism has Christ return after a thousand years of prosperity, and that amillennialism sees the millennium in symbolic terms; he says most Christian religious groups have opted for amillennialism. Sean Durbin says Augustine's City of God played a crucial role in transforming the millennium from a material to a symbolic entity, and Pieter de Villiers says amillennialism is commonly understood as the result of the influence of Origen and Augustine, who rejected a literal reading of the thousand years.
The Decalogue assumes the existence of o: The Decalogue assumes the existence of other gods (see Exod 20:3).
The Decalogue is going to be repeated in: The Decalogue is going to be repeated in Deuteronomy, chapter five. And there are some minor variations. Specifically you'll see that the rationale for observing the Sabbath is different.
The Encyclopaedia Judaica's article on t: The Encyclopaedia Judaica's article on the Book of the Covenant says the name derives from Exodus 24:7 and is usually taken to refer to the material in Exodus 20:22–23:33, which it divides into cultic ordinances, legal prescriptions, religious and moral instructions, and an epilogue. Brown's Bible Odyssey article places the collection at Exodus 20:22–23:19, and Edenburg's chapter in the Oxford Handbook of Biblical Law says scholars are divided on whether it comprises all of Exodus 20:22–24:1 or only parts of that block. The NABRE notes say it contains both apodictic (absolute) and casuistic (conditional) laws, and Hayes's Yale lectures call casuistic “if/then” law the common form of law in the ancient Near East. The Coogan and Chapman chapter summary says that, unlike its Near Eastern antecedents, the collection also regulates worship, and that its directives are not comprehensive.
The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on Hag: The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on Hagar says contemporary critical scholarship regards the first Hagar tradition as predominantly J, with Priestly insertions, and the second as entirely E; that both accounts involve Hagar's banishment, an angel with an oracle and a well; and that it has been suggested that two independent versions of her banishment once existed, though the entry notes that the difficulties of the two accounts are lessened if they are considered separate crystallizations of the Hagar–Ishmael saga. It notes that, read together, the chronology makes Ishmael more than 14 years old at his banishment. The New American Bible's notes say that in the present Elohist (?) story Ishmael is obviously a little boy, not much older than Isaac. John Noble's study of Ishmael in the Priestly tradition describes the accounts of Hagar and Ishmael in Genesis 16 and 21 as often attributed to the Yahwist or the Elohist.
The English transliteration of a Hebrew: The English transliteration of a Hebrew word whose literal meaning is “adversary.” In the OT, the figure of Satan appears only three times (Job 1-2; Zech 3:1-2; 1Chr 21:1).
The Genesis narrative records both attem: The Genesis narrative records both attempted sexual perversity and gross inhospitality (Gen 19:1-11).
The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary calls: The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary calls Romans 1:26–27 the most extensive biblical reference to homosexual acts and says they are mentioned as one example of the perversions that follow when humankind refuses to give glory and thanks to God. William Loader's Bible Odyssey article says Paul chose same-sex relations as his example, and that it represented pagan depravity to him and his readers. Bruce Wells's Bible Odyssey article says Paul does seem to call homosexual behavior by men and women unnatural, but that his main point is to denounce idolatry. On “unnatural”, Loader says that in Paul's world it was unnatural and shameful for a man to take a passive role or a woman an active one, and Jimmy Hoke's Bible Odyssey article says Paul uses the same phrase Roman writers used to associate such practices with foreign deviance. Dale Martin's Yale lectures, on ancient sexual hierarchy generally, say that in ancient Judaism and Christianity it was considered sex “against nature” for a woman to penetrate a man. Loader adds that Paul's concern is not only pederasty but also consensual sex.
The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary defin: The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary defines a concubine as a marital associate of a man secondary to his wife, says the barren wives Sarah, Leah and Rachel sometimes gave their handmaidens to their husbands as concubines to bear children, and says the Torah legally guaranteed the rights of a Hebrew girl sold into concubinage (Exodus 21:7–11); the NABRE note on Exodus 21:8 explains “designated her” as intended her as a wife of second rank. D. Bergant's New Catholic Encyclopedia article describes Hagar, Bilhah and Zilpah as maidservants offered to husbands as surrogates, and Carol Meyers's Encyclopaedia Judaica article says that in most instances a second wife or a concubine was taken because the first wife did not produce offspring. Wil Gafney's Bible Odyssey article says Israelites practised two-tiered marriage, in which the children of a pilegesh, often mistranslated “concubine”, were not entitled to an inheritance, and that Hagar, though enslaved, became Abraham's wife, the same status Sarah had. Susanne Scholz's Bible Odyssey article says contemporary feminist scholars argue convincingly that pilegesh is more complicated than the English “concubine” suggests, and that several texts suggest a pilegesh was an enslaved woman whose function was to please her master sexually and produce his children.
The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary lists: The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary lists Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene as separate women among the seven women named Mary in the New Testament, “unless two or more are identical”. Kristin Swenson says Magdalene refers to a town in Galilee, which should distinguish her from Mary of Bethany, near Jerusalem. Elizabeth Schrader, who argues in the Harvard Theological Review that a text of John without Martha would strongly imply that Mary of Bethany was Mary Magdalene, writes that Mary Ann Beavis and Mark Goodacre had already challenged the relatively recent scholarly tendency to draw a clear line between them. Beavis says early Christians sometimes confused the two Marys because of their similar names, that Eastern Christians resisted the conflation and traditionally regarded them as distinct saints, and that in the West Gregory the Great identified the sinner of Luke 7 with Mary Magdalene rather than with Mary of Bethany. Swenson and Dan Clanton, by contrast, say Gregory's sermon equated Mary of Bethany with Mary Magdalene as well.
The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says: The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says Hades is the realm of the dead in Greek mythology, used in the Septuagint to translate Sheol and in the New Testament for the abode of the dead, though in one passage, Luke 16:23, it is a place of torment, and that Gehenna is the word the New Testament commonly uses for the place where sinners are punished after death. The New American Bible's note on 2 Peter 2:4 calls Tartarus a term borrowed from Greek mythology for the infernal regions, and Robert Fastiggi's entry in the International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences notes that the word appears there. Carol Zaleski's Britannica article and Kim Papaioannou's article both say Gehenna appears twelve times in the New Testament; Papaioannou counts seven in Matthew, three in Mark and one each in Luke and James, all but James's on the lips of Jesus. David Sim's article in HTS Teologiese Studies reads Matthew's Hades as the Greek equivalent of Gehenna.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says Mary Magdalene is mentioned first in every listing of Jesus's female disciples and seems to have led a group of women who followed and served Jesus from the start of his ministry in Galilee and provided for it from their own means; Luke 8:2 describes her as one from whom seven demons had gone out, which the dictionary reads as healing from some serious affliction. It features her foremost as a witness to Jesus's death and to the empty tomb. Jane Webster's Bible Odyssey article likewise says the gospels have her travel with Jesus and the disciples, provide for them and see Jesus crucified. Kristin Swenson's Bible Odyssey article says she appears in all four gospels and that they are in remarkable agreement about her presence at the death, burial and resurrection of Jesus, and that only Luke mentions her before Jesus's death. N. E. Müller van Velden's article in Acta Theologica adds that Luke, unlike Mark and Matthew, does not name her at the crucifixion, and that John mentions no women at the burial. Dale Martin's Yale lectures say he thinks women were part of Jesus's inner circle, citing the resurrection narratives and the presence of Mary Magdalene.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says satan is a Hebrew word whose literal meaning is “adversary”, and that the figure of Satan appears only three times in the Old Testament, in Job 1–2, Zechariah 3:1–2 and 1 Chronicles 21:1. In the first two, it says, he is a member of God's court whose duty is to accuse human beings before God, and is not presented as an enemy of God or as the leader of the demonic forces of evil. Adam Porter's Bible Odyssey article says that in Job 1–2 the noun has the definite article, “the satan”, and should be translated as a title, “the accuser”, and that the accuser is not responsible for evil in the Hebrew Bible, which generally attributes both good and evil to God. Christine Hayes's Yale lectures call the satan of Job a member of the divine council who acts as a kind of prosecuting attorney, and say he is certainly not the devil: there is no such notion in the Hebrew Bible. The New American Bible's note on Job 1:6 calls the satan a member of the heavenly court, “the accuser”, whom later biblical traditions develop as the devil, and its note on Zechariah 3:1 calls the adversary there the prosecuting attorney, a figure in the Lord's heavenly courtroom, whom later tradition understands to be Satan. Shawna Dolansky's Bible Odyssey talk says “the satan” is a job title, not a proper name. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says the noun is applied to human adversaries, as in 1 Samuel 29:4 and 1 Kings 11:14, and that the angel sent to obstruct Balaam in Numbers 22 was chosen for the occasion, as a satan.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says that in the New Testament period it appears that the definition of adultery was extended, so that a husband could also be held responsible for committing adultery against his wife (Matthew 5:32; Mark 10:11; Luke 16:18). Jill Marshall's Bible Odyssey article says that in Matthew 5:27–32 and its parallels Jesus intensifies the Jewish law: even thinking about adultery is a sin, and divorce places a woman in a position that results in adultery. Dale Martin's Yale lecture reads the saying as forbidding even desire for a woman who belongs to another man, which intensifies the Torah rather than doing away with it, and R. F. Collins says Matthew's interpretation of the commandment is similar to the midrashic interpretation of the early rabbinic tradition. A. Andrew Das's Bible Odyssey article says that in Mark 10:10–12 Jesus adds that for either partner to divorce and remarry is adulterous. Eben Scheffler writes that Mark applies the rule to both sexes, while Matthew treats divorce as a male option and regards the divorced woman as the one committing adultery.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says that in the Old Testament adultery had a precise and limited definition, sexual relations between a married or betrothed woman and any man other than her husband, and was a most grievous transgression, to be punished by the death of both parties. Deborah Rooke's Bible Odyssey article calls the definition in much of the Hebrew Bible one-sided: men could have more than one wife, and even for married men sleeping with unmarried or unbetrothed women did not count as adultery; only men who slept with another man's wife or fiancée could be punished for it. Ishay Rosen-Zvi's Jewish Women's Archive article says the paramour's marital status is irrelevant to the case. Donald Slager writes that the woman's status defines whether it is adultery, and that married men had greater sexual freedom than married women, since they could have sex with unpledged virgins and prostitutes with a penalty less than death. Cynthia Edenburg writes that Deuteronomy 22:22 demands of the married woman an uncompromising sexual exclusivity, so that any intercourse between a married woman and a man other than her husband counts as adultery, whether she consented or not.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says that, probably because of its associations with fiery destruction and judgment, the word Gehenna came to be used metaphorically during the intertestamental period for hell or eternal damnation, and that the New Testament uses it only in this way. Meghan Henning's Bible Odyssey article says that in apocalyptic books written between the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, such as 1 Enoch, Gehenna began to be associated with fire, judgment and punishment, so that by the time Mark or Matthew wrote, people already thought of it as a fiery place of punishment. Nicolas Wyatt's article in Numen finds the cosmology later attached to the valley already in 1 Enoch 26–27, where the valley is the place of judgment and not yet a symbol of some transcendent location. The New American Bible's note on Matthew 5:22 says punishment of sinners by fire is found in Jewish apocalyptic literature, but that the name Gehenna is first given to the place of punishment in the New Testament. Kim Papaioannou's article in the Melanesian Journal of Theology reports the common belief that a Gehenna tradition came to full bloom in intertestamental Jewish literature, and argues against it: the valley of 1 Enoch 27 is unnamed, and the Gospels are the earliest writings after Jeremiah to mention Gehenna in an eschatological context.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the Holiness Code of Leviticus prohibits a male, under penalty of death, from lying with another male as a woman does. Christine Hayes's Yale lectures and the chapter summary for Coogan and Chapman's textbook place these chapters in the Holiness Code, a distinct source; Hayes says most scholars think it comes from a different priestly school, designated H, and that Leviticus 18 and 20 list sexual transgressions that defile the land, which will vomit out those who dwell on it. Jan Joosten says 20:13 parallels 18:22 and adds a punishment, and that the verse unambiguously addresses sex between males and has widely been interpreted as a blanket prohibition; he reports Saul Olyan's view that the law was originally aimed at the insertive partner, and proposes his own reading, a prohibition of intercourse with a married man. J. Stiebert says what the phrase means, and how far it reaches, is elusive. Bruce Wells's Bible Odyssey article says that in his opinion no one really knows what “the beds of a woman” means and that most scholars have long read it as the act of lying down, a reading he doubts while saying he is in the minority. David Instone-Brewer's article in HIPHIL Novum argues that it is no longer certain that Leviticus condemned all homoerotic activity.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the commandments are not numbered in the Bible and different systems are used. Brown's Bible Odyssey article names three numbering traditions; in the Jewish one the first “word” is God's self-presentation in Exodus 20:2, while the Christian traditions begin the series at 20:3. The NABRE notes say Catholics and Lutherans traditionally count verses 1–6 as one commandment and verse 17 as two, while the Greek Orthodox and Reformed churches count verses 1–6 as two and verse 17 as one; the two sources place the Anglican tradition differently. Hayes's Yale lectures say the ten are an ideal number found among about thirteen separate statements, numbered differently by Jews and Christians and among Christian denominations, and Brettler says even Jewish tradition offers no single definitive way of making ten.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the plural Elohim implied grandeur in Israelite religion, without any suggestion of multiple identities. David Carr and Marc Zvi Brettler's Bible Odyssey answer says Christian interpreters once saw the Trinity in the plurals of Genesis 1, but that most scholars now agree Genesis 1:26 and similar verses are either a “plural of deliberation” or reflect the idea of a council of semi-divine beings around the God of Israel. Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen says current exegesis regards Genesis 1:26 as a plural of majesty and that contemporary scholarship does not agree with reading such prooftexts as evidence for the Trinity. Dale Martin's Yale lectures say most historical critics would call it certainly wrong to read the doctrine of the Trinity into Genesis.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the text of the Decalogue is given in its entirety twice in the Old Testament with only slight variations, and Brown's Bible Odyssey article names the two versions as Exodus 20:2–17 and Deuteronomy 5:6–21; Brown adds that the replacement tablets given after Moses broke the first set contain a significantly different set of laws (Exodus 34:1–28). Christine Hayes's Yale lectures say the Pentateuch contains three versions of the Decalogue, and that the one in Exodus 34, often called the ritual Decalogue, has very little overlap with the earlier one and concerns festivals, first fruits and firstborn animals; she concludes that there were different traditions about the Decalogue's contents. The chapter summaries for Michael Coogan and Cynthia Chapman's textbook also count three versions, calling the Exodus 34 list a variant tradition known as the Ritual Decalogue.

The HarperCollins Bible Dictionary says the word Gehenna derives from a Hebrew term meaning “valley of Hinnom”, where some kings of Judah practised human sacrifice by fire, and that children were sacrificed as burnt offerings at Topheth. Meghan Henning's Bible Odyssey article says Gehenna is used hardly at all in the Hebrew Bible, where it names an actual place, the Valley of Hinnom, a site of idolatrous worship and child sacrifice. The New American Bible's note on 2 Kings 23:10 places Topheth probably in the Hinnom Valley, where children were apparently immolated to the deity Molech. Robert Fastiggi's entry in the International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences says Gehenna, from the valley of the son of Hinnom, is the biblical word for the state of punishment after death. The Encyclopaedia Judaica says Gehinnom is generally used in Judaism for the place of torment reserved for the wicked after death.
The Heavenly Hosts consist of various ty: The Heavenly Hosts consist of various types of divine beings, including divine messengers; the sun, moon, and stars (Gen 2:1; Ps 148); “holy ones” (Deut 33:2–5, 26–29; Job 15:15; Ps 89:5–18); “sons of God” (Job 38:7; Ps 89:5–18); and the divine council.
The Hebrew Bible refers to many heavenly: The Hebrew Bible refers to many heavenly creatures, calling them “gods” (Gen 6:2; Ps 29:1, Ps 82:6, Ps 86:8, Ps 89:7; Job 1:6)
The Hebrew term mal’akh, like the Greek: The Hebrew term mal’akh, like the Greek term angelos, means “messenger.” The Hebrew Bible uses the term on rare occasion when speaking of a human messenger (Gen 32:3), but typically the term refers to heavenly beings who serve what the Bible regards as the one true God, Yhwh.
The Hebrew term עשרת הדברים, popularly k: The Hebrew term עשרת הדברים, popularly known as “the Ten Commandments,” appears three times: Exodus 34:28; Deut 4:13; 10:4, and is more accurately translated “The Ten Sayings,” which is reflected in the more preferable English term Decalogue, from Greek “deca logoi,” i.e., “Ten Sayings.”
The LXX text of Ps 16:10 does differ fro: The LXX text of Ps 16:10 does differ from the standard Masoretic Text (MT) of the Hebrew, but recent gains in textual criticism demonstrate that we can no longer say whether the LXX or the MT represents a “more original” text, if we can even speak of such a thing.
The Latin word rapio, which in the Latin: The Latin word rapio, which in the Latin Vulgate’s translation of 1 Thessalonians 4:17 translates the Greek harpazo (‘snatch up’), is the etymological starting point for the term ‘Rapture’.
The NABRE introduction says the book was: The NABRE introduction says the book was composed during the persecution carried on by Antiochus IV Epiphanes (167–164 BCE). Christine Hayes's Yale lectures date chapters 7–12 to between 167 and 164 BCE, and the first six chapters perhaps to the end of the third century. Amy Merrill Willis's Bible Odyssey article says the vision of Daniel 8 was written around 167 BCE and that the book's calculations for the end refer to events of 167–164 BCE; its “Did You Know?” box says the Hebrew-Aramaic edition was completed around 163 BCE. The publisher's summary of Coogan and Chapman's introduction says the book was written in the second century BCE, and that scholars place it there. Craig Evans says the dangers Jews faced in the second century BCE, especially under Antiochus IV, led to the writing of the book soon after. Mladen Popović and colleagues note that scholars date Daniel 8–11 on literary-historical grounds to the 160s BCE. The date is not unanimous.
